clinicalPearls: Suspect ZES in patients with severe, recurrent, or refractory peptic ulcers, ulcers in unusual locations (distal duodenum, jejunum), or ulcers with prominent diarrhea that improves with acid suppression.
Chronic secretory diarrhea plus peptic ulcer disease is a classic combination that should prompt gastrin testing.
About 20-30% of gastrinomas occur as part of MEN1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1) — screen for hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumors.
Most gastrinomas arise within the 'gastrinoma triangle' bounded by the cystic duct, junction of the pancreatic head/neck, and duodenal junction.
Fasting serum gastrin should be measured off proton pump inhibitors when clinically feasible, since acid suppression can falsely elevate gastrin.
A markedly elevated fasting gastrin with an inappropriately low gastric pH strongly supports the diagnosis.
Roughly half of gastrinomas are malignant with a tendency for lymph node and hepatic metastases at diagnosis.
Somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g., DOTATATE PET) is the preferred modality for tumor localization given high sensitivity.
harrison.pathophysiology: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), most often located in the duodenum or pancreas, that drives unregulated gastric acid hypersecretion. The resulting profound acid load overwhelms mucosal defenses and inactivates pancreatic enzymes, producing severe/recurrent peptic ulceration and secretory diarrhea with malabsorption. A substantial minority of cases occur in association with MEN1, reflecting a hereditary predisposition to multiple endocrine tumors.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of chronic secretory diarrhea (VIPoma, carcinoid syndrome)
Retained gastric antrum syndrome after prior gastric surgery
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum gastrin — markedly elevated levels raise suspicion for gastrinoma
Gastric pH measurement — low pH with high gastrin confirms inappropriate acid-driven hypergastrinemia
Secretin stimulation test — paradoxical rise in gastrin supports the diagnosis when basal levels are equivocal
Upper endoscopy — assesses ulcer burden, location, and mucosal complications
Somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g., DOTATATE PET/CT) — preferred for primary tumor and metastasis localization
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI abdomen) — evaluates tumor size, local invasion, and hepatic metastases
Endoscopic ultrasound — useful for detecting small pancreatic/duodenal lesions
Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone, prolactin — screen for coexisting MEN1
redFlags: Multiple or recurrent ulcers despite adequate acid-suppressive therapy
Ulcers in atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum)
Evidence of hepatic or nodal metastases at diagnosis
Signs of MEN1 (hypercalcemia, pituitary symptoms) suggesting hereditary syndrome
Complications of ulcer disease such as perforation or bleeding
Severe secretory diarrhea causing dehydration or electrolyte derangement
pitfalls: Failing to hold proton pump inhibitors (when safe to do so) before gastrin testing, leading to false-positive hypergastrinemia
Attributing recurrent ulcers solely to H. pylori or NSAIDs without considering gastrinoma in refractory cases
Overlooking associated MEN1 features, delaying recognition of a hereditary tumor syndrome
Relying on gastrin level alone without confirming inappropriate acid hypersecretion
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends primarily on tumor biology and extent of disease at diagnosis; localized, resectable gastrinomas carry a favorable long-term outlook, while metastatic disease (especially hepatic spread) is associated with reduced survival. Effective acid suppression has greatly reduced ulcer-related morbidity, shifting long-term outcome toward tumor-related factors.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Neuroendocrine Tumors of the Gastrointestinal Tract and Pancreas (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome)
